decisions.reason: “Fight” keeps the brutal-battle sense in more direct prose.
The past perfect fits the flash’s arrival before the observers noticed it.
“As one” naturally conveys the streaks tearing through the air together.
The streaks still travel side by side across the stated distance and hit the battlefield.
“Fireballs” preserves the image while avoiding the awkward “balls of fire.”
Overlapping explosions preserve the layered roar and resulting heat.
Seeing death coming preserves the source’s imminent-danger image.
The shock still makes them forget the pain; the tighter phrasing keeps the effect.
The source says he gave up everything; SOL’s “given up” drops that emphasis.
Watching death bear down preserves the scene without the strained “stared death in the face.”
“Now-melted white hair” keeps the contrast between his youth and present condition.
“With those words echoing” keeps the sense and reads naturally.
Removing “a” before fate preserves the meaning in idiomatic English.
The conjunction preserves the sequence without changing the invocation or glance skyward.
The omitted article does not alter whose enemies the fireballs target.
“The earth heaved” naturally conveys the ground turning over.
“Words of praise” preserves the chanting of the Lord of Heaven’s doctrine.
“Did not stop for a single moment” keeps the source’s uninterrupted advance.
“Roused everyone from their exhaustion” preserves the effect without the stiff “minds of all those sunk.”
The disciples’ stand and arrows halt the coalition’s retreat as defeat threatens.
“Knew it instinctively” preserves the source’s instinctive recognition.
SOL replaces the shouts likened to screams with shouting oneself hoarse, changing the image.
The weapon’s sound cutting through the air preserves the chilling whistle in natural English.
The sentence retains the old man, the flesh, and his scream; the omitted name is established nearby.
“Make sense of” naturally preserves Taishan’s failure to understand the shout in time.
The weapons still strike before the attackers can act and cleave their necks and chests.
The actions are unchanged, and the revised order reads smoothly.
“Caught with his mouth open” adds a sense of being caught off guard absent from the source.
The subdued voice is preserved; the following dialogue makes “replied” unnecessary.
The shorter wording preserves the complaint about an old man suffering at his age.
The shorter ellipsis preserves the pause and exclamation.
The ongoing action is preserved in a cleaner participial phrase.
“From … to … and back” preserves the back-and-forth glance in idiomatic English.
“Blazing” intensifies the source’s eyes glinting; BASE keeps the milder image.
“Come through a battle like this” keeps the question’s meaning and sounds natural.
“Slashed” accurately conveys being cut by a sword in the fight.
Wishing his sworn brothers were here preserves his longing for their presence.
“Great Sir” follows the established rendering for 대인.
“For no particular reason” preserves the casual, unmotivated glance.
“Last sight” naturally preserves the possibility that this is the last thing he sees.
“Doubted his eyes” keeps the source’s disbelief in idiomatic English.
Dropping the initial “And” does not change the contrast or the reason for his surprise.
“Unsettling” preserves his distrust of the companions without changing the fact.
The present-tense phrasing preserves what catches his eye in the moment.
“Would remain so” preserves the prediction in natural English.
Snow scattering in the figures’ wake preserves the windblown snow and their rapid movement.
“Ran down” preserves their movement down the slope without changing the image.
“Wherever it went” preserves the wave’s undiminished radiance.
The cry sweeps across the battlefield as the guards race downhill and gather speed.
“One word” naturalizes the Korean’s two-character phrase for “victory” without changing its sense.
The commander’s voice still rings clearly in their ears.
The Korean says no one answered Jeong Hogun’s question; SOL makes it sound as if they answered him personally.
SOL turns their rising aura into an answer, while the source says there was no answer, only a growing presence.
The revised tense preserves the passage of more than a hundred years.
The source identifies the Zhu hero who ascended the throne; SOL’s “a hero” weakens that specific reference.
“Selected and dressed” preserves the selection and golden robes and armor.
“Thrown … into turmoil” preserves the disruption of the imperial court in natural speech.
“Low-set helmets” naturally describes helmets worn low over the eyes.
The wording preserves the route through Liaoning and Hebei to Gansu.
The sentence is retained at the start of the following hunk rather than omitted.
The sentence preserves the guards’ exhaustion and bodies not being made of steel.
“Resolve” conveys ordinary determination here; the source is not invoking the System attribute.
“For as long as they lived” preserves that they would never forget the command.
The Son of Heaven they met preserves the source’s fragment without adding “the sight of.”
The smile and final command remain, and the pronoun refers clearly to the Son of Heaven.
“Cried out” avoids the awkward “with force” while preserving the forceful shout.
“Drawn” adds a specific action; the source only says the weapons appeared and flashed.
“Qi” follows the project’s rendering for martial energy.
The wave still sweeps away everything in its path.
“The instant” preserves the timing of the arrows striking the enemy ranks.
“Changed the course of the battle” preserves the battlefield’s shift in natural English.
